description: I'm Manuel Guilherme, a software and security engineer in Blumenau, Brazil. I build with NASA data, Rust, Python and JavaScript. Our project, moonseal, finds the right day to land at the Moon's south pole from JPL Horizons and LRO LOLA data, tells whether a lander there would have a signal to Earth, checked live against NASA's Deep Space Network, and seals each finding, post-quantum signed, on Solana devnet. Looking for: planetary science, mission design, radio links and data visualization.
summary:
moonseal is a free web planner for landing at the Moon's south pole. There the Sun barely rises and Earth hides behind the mountains, so a lander that touches down on the wrong day can lose power or go silent: in March 2025 the lander Athena tipped over in a cold crater and its 10-day mission ended in less than 13 hours.

For any site near the pole, moonseal checks every hour of 2026 and 2027 against the real terrain, using NASA JPL Horizons and LRO LOLA data, and marks the good days to land: sunlight for power and Earth in view for radio. It ranks the south-pole sites on power, water ice (LRO Diviner) and radio, and tells whether a lander there would actually have a signal to Earth, checking its math live against NASA's Deep Space Network.

When you find a good day, moonseal signs the finding with a post-quantum signature (ML-DSA-65), and a program on Solana's test network verifies it on chain, so anyone can check later what was found and when.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

- The good days to land. For a curated site, or any point you tap, moonseal tests every hour of 2026 and 2027: is the Sun above the real skyline (power), and is Earth above it (direct radio)? Choose a stay of a week, two weeks or two months, and the timeline marks in green every hour you could land without a night longer than the battery or a radio blackout longer than your limit. "Find the next good time to land" jumps straight to the next one.

- The south-pole sites, ranked. On power (sunlight), water (where ice can last, from LRO Diviner: under the site, or the distance to the nearest cold trap) and radio (Earth in view), each counting the same, over every hour of 2026 and 2027. MoonDAO's Moon Base Zero comes first.

- A comparison you can act on. The same dates at the other sites, side by side; a skyline view from the site with the Sun and Earth on it; a field guide per site (temperatures and ice stability from LRO Diviner, gravity from GRAIL, LRO images, nearby named features), each with its source.

- Seals what you found. Press Seal on a site: the finding (site, good time to land, stay, what the planner measured, the NASA data) is signed with ML-DSA-65 (NIST FIPS 204) in the browser, and the moonseal program on Solana verifies the signature on chain. The finding's bytes stay in the public transactions; the seal id is sha256(key, signature, finding). Change one letter and the seal no longer matches.

- Earth in view, computed on Solana. "Ask Solana" on a site sends the point, the hour, the sub-Earth point and distance (JPL Horizons) and the point's skyline (LOLA) to a second program on devnet, which computes Earth's elevation inside the transaction and logs IN VIEW or HIDDEN. It agrees with the planner to 0.000001° over 70 test cases. Program GKs2P6bWKSnyCzrTsc7LcEp7MjUdCE4RaDYnynNiTWB5; examples:

https://explorer.solana.com/tx/5wUzwwhJHEporAqHfxnJJoXFA6ryFuPCqoppzjJbn5ZzSDvFUS2tFYCzwAz3hn2ruUFXfnjmMsdB1wFZ8Rr97JEf?cluster=devnet https://explorer.solana.com/tx/aJcU1Qvn9nMtb7SsSX4x3hvF6j4FPYDJ9rppqJxFwPUw8ChDFMd1o7MYdjpkxwCcxqBzkojNhDekh4c6TC2yyR6?cluster=devnet

- Signal to Earth, checked against NASA's dishes live. Earth over the skyline is not enough: a dish on Earth must also have the Moon in its sky. For any site and hour moonseal says whether a lander there would have a signal: Earth over its skyline, and one of NASA's three Deep Space Network complexes (Goldstone, Madrid, Canberra) with the Moon at least 10° up; then a link budget for a reference X-band lander radio (5 W, 10 dBi) to a 34 m dish: about -110 dBm, 6.6 to 8.5 Mb/s depending on the Earth-Moon distance. The Moon's place in each complex's sky stays within 0.26° of JPL Horizons over 2026 and 2027; some complex has the Moon 97.9% of the hours, with gaps of at most 2 hours. On the first screen a live strip reads NASA's public DSN Now feed: which Moon spacecraft a NASA dish is working this minute, and whether our math puts the Moon in that dish's sky. On 15 November 2026 at 22:59 UTC it read: Goldstone dish DSS23 pointed at Danuri (Korea's lunar orbiter); our math, Moon 28° up at Goldstone: agrees.

WHY IT MATTERS

On 6 March 2025 the lander Athena reached the south pole about 800 feet outside its target zone and came to rest on its side in a crater. Intuitive Machines said the direction of the Sun, the orientation of its solar panels and the cold in the crater meant it would not recharge; a mission planned for 10 days lasted less than 13 hours (Scientific American: https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/athena-lunar-lander-declared-dead-on-the-moon/). moonseal would not have prevented that landing error. The story shows how unforgiving light is at the pole, where a few hundred meters and a few hours decide whether a lander has power and a voice.

HOW IT WORKS

- Sun and Earth positions: JPL Horizons (DE441) gives the sub-solar and sub-Earth points on the Moon, hourly, 2026-2027, in the same Moon-fixed frame as the LOLA terrain. The browser turns them into azimuth and elevation for any site, including Earth's parallax. Checked against direct Horizons queries at 4 sites for every hour of 2026: elevation error at most 0.0007°.

- The skyline: LOLA LDEM_75S_240M (240 m/pixel), ray-cast over 360° with the Moon's curvature, so a high ridge sees past the edge of the sphere. A body is up when its centre clears the skyline.

- Checks: the in-browser planner reproduces the Python engine exactly for 2026 at 5 sites (sunlight %, Earth %, longest night, longest blackout). A dropped pin's skyline, ray-cast in the browser, is within 0.06°-0.8° RMS of the engine at the curated sites.

- The picture: LRO LROC WAC color and LOLA relief on the globe; the polar cap is real LOLA geometry with shadows ray-marched toward the real Sun; NASA PGDA 5 m/pixel site models for close-ups.

- On chain: an ML-DSA-65 key (1,952 B) and signature (3,309 B) do not fit one Solana transaction, and one verification costs about 3.4M compute units, above the 1.4M cap. So the data goes into a buffer in chunks and is verified in stages: 11-12 transactions, each at most 1,076,302 compute units and 1,155 bytes. Signatures from the browser (@noble/post-quantum 0.7.1) and from Java (BouncyCastle 1.81) both verify; tampered ones are rejected. Live on Solana devnet (program 3ieMTX6qafSSwMgdeu8QGCRox1bK84emdwEuD6RShbd7, registry 2QYth8MJoLCdRgWckS6QTcjjvBoESFcsohRrLxeAoQN6):

- a sealed landing-site finding (Moon Base Zero, 15 Nov 2026): VERIFIED https://explorer.solana.com/tx/5UJiJvxASdziQg2SHoQTpEbPpyfZSNgNcXxkxDtDMH8kcN94M8j3gWVHxQH3s8qgQusgkPwJggZxhSZV17Keao2d?cluster=devnet · the finding's bytes (second part) https://explorer.solana.com/tx/34APcddYHTU6x9iGZbuW8YiK2aBm8tEU8a62oMfAkcDKLSjx697opD56kE9FQy8G9P9YnMBKSArBdZcELL3uDAEv?cluster=devnet

- command gate, authorized: https://explorer.solana.com/tx/3LzG1NYBPBG5YLJiHYa5rQYzeEuq2kUDXV38ZDmPzF6X63UbNBuq8bkHZ9YcykxwYEqQLLCWiLTzsSQ1CdYPXvMV?cluster=devnet

- refused, valid signature from a key not on the list: https://explorer.solana.com/tx/52Pjd7wNHzd3h6YEUDDiTA62BYE7t4FL38XM1aos2NcLtGb8SekAkR9rp5RWDbdHDermcHAfzcnSHHKnUm643B7i?cluster=devnet

- refused, replayed command: https://explorer.solana.com/tx/4f7jrwPysLARj44g5BQ2rcQj78Lzis97ot2LrfmrENjXGyqRHSG9e8A3yEh4wL9nT84wWibtqwk9YVGURAS5L4j6?cluster=devnet

- Why a chain at all: a base with no single owner cannot keep its list of who may command it on someone's server. On Solana the list, the counter and the record of every decision are public, and the team's ML-DSA key, not Solana's own ed25519, is the root of trust.

RESULTS WORTH SHOWING (2026, CENTRE OF THE BODY ABOVE THE SKYLINE)

- Connecting Ridge: sunlight 91.2%, Earth in view 50.9%, longest night 101 h

- Malapert Massif: sunlight 81.0%, Earth in view 100% (worst-hour margin 0.10°), longest night 277 h

- de Gerlache Rim 2: sunlight 22.3%, Earth in view 50.1%, longest night 688 h

- Peak Near Shackleton: sunlight 16.9%, Earth in view 33.6%, longest night 642 h

- Moon Base Zero (MoonDAO): sunlight 85.5%, Earth in view 50.8%, longest night 116 h

Small moves matter: Moon Base Zero's centre is 402 m from our Connecting Ridge point and gets 85.5% sunlight against 91.2%.

WHAT WE HOPE TO ACHIEVE

A free, open planner any lander team can use to pick its landing hour, and a pattern for commanding a base that many groups share: the base, not any one operator, decides who may command it.

TOOLS

HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no framework), three.js 0.187.0, Python (data pipeline), Rust (the Solana program), Bun, @noble/post-quantum 0.7.1, BouncyCastle 1.81, Solana devnet, Remotion (the video).

HONEST LIMITATIONS

- 240 m terrain: no boulders or local slopes below that scale. "Signal" means Earth over the skyline, a NASA dish with the Moon at least 10° up, and a free-space link budget for a stated reference radio; DSN scheduling, each dish's own horizon mask and relay satellites are out of scope. The live strip shows what NASA's feed reports; when no Moon spacecraft is on a dish, it says so.

- Malapert's continuous Earth view rests on a 0.10° margin.

- The on-chain verifier is new code: tested against two independent implementations, not audited. It runs on Solana devnet, the test network.

- Hackathon prototype; not a NASA product, not flight-qualified.

LIVE SITE AND CODE

- Live site: https://moonseal.vercel.app

- Code (MIT): https://github.com/Galmanus/moonseal
